meta.description: No, Benjamin Franklin never said democracy is two wolves and a lamb voting on lunch. The line is an anonymous modern saying first printed in 1987.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Democracy is two wolves and a lamb voting on what to have for lunch'?
meta.ogDescription: Franklin never wrote it. Etymologists trace this anonymous quip only to 1987 — nearly 200 years after his death.

answer.label: Not Benjamin Franklin — an anonymous modern saying
answer.sourceLine: This is a 20th-century political quip, not a Franklin line. Etymologist Barry Popik traces the exact wording only to 1987 — in the journal Nomos, credited to an unknown author — nearly two centuries after Franklin died in 1790. It appears in none of his writings, and the Franklin credit only spread online around 2000.

source.heading: Where it really comes from
source.excerpt: Democracy is two wolves and a lamb, voting on what to have for lunch.
trail: Etymologist Barry Popik documents the earliest print appearance in 1987, in the journal Nomos: Studies in Spontaneous Order, with the author unknown — followed by 1989 and 1990 newspaper and Usenet citations.
WIST Quotations flags the line as spurious, noting the word “lunch” only entered English in the 1820s — decades after Franklin’s death in 1790.
A Check Your Fact review found no instance in Franklin’s writings or the National Archives database, and quotes a Baylor historian who could not locate it in Franklin’s papers.
source.excerptNote: As printed in the journal Nomos (1987), page 32, with authorship noted as unknown — the earliest documented appearance located by etymologist Barry Popik. A frequent modern companion line, “Liberty is a well-armed lamb contesting the vote,” appears to be even more recent and also anonymous.

source.rightsNote: The exact wording is an anonymous modern saying with no identifiable author — first documented only in 1987. Because its origin is unknown, no copyright or public-domain status can honestly be asserted.

author.name: Benjamin Franklin
author.heading: Why Franklin?
author.bio: Benjamin Franklin was a printer, scientist, diplomat and one of the Founding Fathers of the United States. His genuine aphorisms — many from Poor Richard’s Almanack — made him a byword for pithy wisdom, which is exactly why unrelated modern one-liners get retroactively pinned on him. This wolves-and-lamb quip is one of them: catchy, political, and entirely absent from his actual work.

misattribution.heading: How Franklin got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook viral misattribution: a punchy modern political line back-dated onto a Founding Father to lend it authority. The Franklin credit is not old — it spread online only around 2000.

items.why: The line appears in none of Franklin’s writings and is absent from the National Archives database; a Baylor historian could not locate it in his papers. Check Your Fact rates it false ↗.
The same quip is variously pinned on other founders, none with any source. It is an anonymous 20th-century saying, first printed in 1987 per Barry Popik’s research ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The closest genuine Franklin sentiment is a 1773 line — “if you make yourself a Sheep, the Wolves will eat you” — but the wolves-and-lamb-voting quip is anonymous and modern, documented no earlier than the late 1980s ↗.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The image is vivid and instantly graspable: majority rule as predators outvoting prey. That makes it a favorite in libertarian and gun-rights rhetoric, usually paired with the follow-on “Liberty is a well-armed lamb contesting the vote.”
Attaching it to Benjamin Franklin gives a modern talking point the borrowed gravity of a Founder — which is precisely the mechanism that manufactures fake quotes.
context.pull: Two wolves and a lamb, voting on lunch — vivid, quotable, and entirely un-Franklin.
